Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one has arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply 10 questions about the past seven days; it helps us spot anything from normal baby-blues to something that might need a little extra support. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger. Nothing you say will sound silly or shocking—I’ve heard it all, and my only goal is to keep you safe and well. When you’re ready, we’ll move through the questions at your pace. Shall we begin?

1. Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—would you say as much as always, not quite so much, definitely not so much, or not at all?

Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but when my husband makes a silly face or the dog does something goofy, I’ll still crack up. So… “not quite so much,” I guess.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’ve been able to laugh, just maybe not quite as often as I used to—so “not quite so much.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I still look forward to stuff—like my morning coffee or when my sister comes over—but the excitement is a little muted compared to before. So I’d say “yes, but not as much as I used to.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
I don’t really beat myself up—if the baby spits up a bunch or I’m running late, I figure it happens. I’d say “no, most of the time I haven’t blamed myself.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
A little bit—sometimes I’ll suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing when he’s napping, even though I just checked. It’s not constant, so I’d pick “no, not much.”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
I haven’t felt truly scared or panicky—maybe just a quick flutter of worry if he coughs or startles, but it passes right away. So I’d say “no, not at all.”
Things have been getting on top of me

A few times, when he’s cluster-feeding and the dishes pile up, I’ve thought, “Whoa, this is a lot,” but I can still take a breath and handle it step-by-step. So I’d choose “yes, but I’ve been able to cope.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, I’ve actually been sleeping pretty well—when the baby gives me a three-hour stretch, I drift right off. So I’d say “no, not at all.”
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t felt sad or miserable. I get a little tired or frustrated sometimes, but overall I’m still smiling at the baby’s goofy faces.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I really haven’t cried much—maybe one evening when I was extra tired, but it was just a couple tears and then I felt fine.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You shared that laughter still comes easily when your husband or dog is silly, though the sparkle feels slightly dimmer than before baby, and you still anticipate small pleasures like coffee or your sister's visits, just with a little less excitement. You notice occasional fleeting worries about your baby breathing but no panic, and while cluster-feeding plus dishes can feel overwhelming, you reliably calm yourself and cope step-by-step. You deny persistent sadness, frequent crying, sleep-interruption from low mood, self-blame, or any thoughts of self-harm, noting only one tired tearful evening that quickly passed.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 5, Risk Level: Depression not likely
**Reasoning:** This score falls below the 8-point threshold where postpartum depression screening typically flags further action. Core DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset require ≥5 symptoms (including either depressed mood or loss of interest/pleasure) most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks, plus clinically significant distress or impairment. Your report shows intact pleasure (<quote>still smiling at the baby's goofy faces</quote>), no persistent low mood, no fatigue beyond normal new-parent tiredness, no sleep disruption due to mood, no guilt, and zero self-harm ideation. Occasional worries about infant safety are normative postpartum vigilance rather than pathological <med>anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine paediatric and six-week postpartum check-ins; mention any mood changes
2. Keep balanced rest: nap when baby naps, accept help with chores, stay hydrated and nourished
3. Schedule a brief re-screen if distress increases or persists beyond two weeks
4. Share resources: local new-parent groups, 24-hr postpartum support lines, partner or family respite
5. Return immediately if you notice escalating sadness, hopelessness, intrusive thoughts, or self-harm ideas
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 5: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Self-report on 10-item EPDS analogue

Symptoms endorsed  
- Mildly reduced enjoyment / anticipatory pleasure (Q1, Q2)  
- Transient, situational “overwhelm” when demands spike; able to re-regulate (Q6)  
- Occasional intrusive worry about infant safety, not meeting panic threshold (Q4)

Symptoms denied  
Persistent low mood, crying spells, sleep-mood linkage, guilt/self-blame, panic, self-harm ideation (Q3, Q5, Q7–Q10)

Pattern  
Sub-threshold for core depressive or anxiety clusters; no safety concerns identified.

Screening significance  
Current profile does not suggest elevated risk for major postpartum depression or anxiety disorder; routine paediatric/primary follow-up and education on symptom escalation recommended.
